Why 80% of Women Wear the Wrong Bra Size (and How to Fix It)

If a bra feels uncomfortable, most people assume their body is the problem. In reality, multiple studies have found that roughly 70–80% of women wear a band that is too loose and a cup that is too small . The good news: the fix takes about five minutes and a soft measuring tape.

This guide explains where the "80%" figure comes from, why the wrong size is so common, the symptoms to look for, and how to use our bra size calculator to find a fit that actually works.

Where Does the 80% Figure Come From?

The "80%" figure is shorthand for a well-replicated finding across multiple peer-reviewed studies: the great majority of women wear a bra that does not match their professionally measured size . The most-cited evidence includes:

  • McGhee & Steele (2010) — cross-sectional study of 104 Australian women. 85% were wearing an ill-fitting bra based on professional fit criteria, and self-selection (or self-measurement) performed no better than chance at finding the correct size ( doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2010.03.003 ).
  • Greenbaum, Heslop, Morris & Dunn (2003) — UK clinical study of 102 women referred for breast-reduction surgery. 100% wore the wrong size , with the band underestimated by a mean of 4 inches (range 2–10 in.) and the cup over- or under-estimated by an average of 3 sizes ( doi:10.1016/S0007-1226(03)00122-X ).
  • Coltman, Steele & McGhee (2018) — Australian study of 309 women across four breast-size categories. Only ~10% of bras passed a professional fit assessment ; cups, front band, and straps were the most-failed components ( doi:10.1177/0887302X17743814 ).
  • Haworth et al. (2022) — pre-clinical study of 24 larger-breasted UK women. 100% failed the bra-fit assessment in their usual bra and 67% still failed after a professional fitting, showing that even expert in-store fitting is not a guarantee ( doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2022.103701 ).

Taken together, the published literature puts the true range at roughly 70%–100% of women wearing the wrong bra size, with the most common errors being a band that is too loose and a cup that is too small. The exact percentage depends on the country, the cohort, and the fit criteria used — but the headline conclusion is the same in every study.

Note that "wrong size" in these studies is defined by professional fit criteria — band snugness, wire placement, breast containment — not by self-reported size. Most of the women in the studies thought their bra fit fine.

Why It Happens: The 5 Most Common Reasons

1. Sizing is not taught. Most women buy a bra once, early in life, and stick with that size for a decade or more. The truth is that your size changes with weight, pregnancy, hormonal cycles, and aging. Re-measuring every 6–12 months is the norm, not the exception.

2. Vanity sizing in stores. A 36D in a department store often measures closer to a 34DD. Retailers expand band sizes to make shoppers feel smaller. This is a mirror-image of "vanity sizing" in clothing: the label looks friendlier than the body.

3. The "tight band = uncomfortable" myth. Many people add to the band to relieve pressure. In reality, the band is supposed to do 80–90% of the work. If the band rides up your back, it's too loose, not too tight.

4. Scoop and swoosh is skipped. Stepping into a bra (instead of fastening behind the back) and not scooping breast tissue fully into the cup leaves the cup under-filled and the band carrying extra weight. This is the single most common fitting mistake.

5. Sister sizes aren't used. If the band of a 34DD feels snug, the natural assumption is to try 36DD. The correct answer is 36D (a sister size) — same cup volume, looser band. Skipping the sister-size rule leads people to buy a cup that's too small for them.

Health Effects of an Ill-Fitting Bra

A poorly fitting bra is rarely dangerous, but it is a daily source of preventable discomfort. Common symptoms include:

  • Back, neck, and shoulder pain — straps and cups that don't carry weight correctly transfer load to the upper trapezius and thoracic spine.
  • Digging or chafing under the arms and across the back — usually a sign of a too-small cup or too-tight band.
  • Straps that constantly fall off the shoulders — a sign that the band is too loose (the band is supposed to anchor the bra, not the straps).
  • Cup spillage or wrinkling — too-small or too-large cup, respectively.
  • Underwire pressing on breast tissue — the wire should sit on the ribcage behind the breast, not on the breast.
  • Headaches and breast tenderness — chronic over-compression of breast tissue has been linked to recurring mastalgia in some studies.

None of these are inevitable. A well-fitting bra should feel "barely there" — supportive without compressing, lifting without digging.

The 5-Minute Fix: How to Use the Calculator

The fastest path to a correct size is two measurements and a calculator. Here's the full workflow:

  1. Measure your underbust. Wrap a soft measuring tape snugly around your ribcage, directly under your breasts. Round to the nearest whole inch. This is your band size.
  2. Measure your bust. Wrap the tape loosely around the fullest part of your bust. Round to the nearest whole inch. Do not compress.
  3. Open the calculator. Go to the bra size calculator at the top of the home page and enter both numbers.
  4. Read the output. The calculator returns your size in US, UK, EU, FR, and AU. Save the result as a note on your phone.
  5. Try on a bra in that size. If it doesn't feel right, consult the sister size chart and try a band up or down with the corresponding cup adjustment.

Total time: 5 minutes. Re-measure every 6–12 months, or any time your weight changes by 5+ pounds.

What "Right Fit" Actually Looks Like

A well-fitting bra has five signs to check for:

  • Band: sits level all the way around, parallel to the floor. You can fit two fingers under it, but not more.
  • Straps: stay on your shoulders without digging in. They carry roughly 10–20% of breast weight.
  • Cups: breast tissue is fully contained. No spillage at the top, sides, or center. No wrinkling of fabric.
  • Underwire (if present): lies flat against your ribcage, behind the breast. Does not press on breast tissue.
  • Gore (center panel): sits flat against your sternum. A gap here means the cup is too small or the band is too loose.

If two or more of these fail, your size is wrong — or your current bra has stretched out and needs to be replaced. (Yes, bras have a lifespan. Most last 6–12 months of regular wear before the band loses elasticity.)

What to Do If the Calculator Number Doesn't Match Your Current Bra

If you've always worn 36B and the calculator says 34D, you're not alone. Here is a sensible plan:

  1. Order one bra in the calculator's size. Try it on at home with the scoop-and-swoosh technique (lean forward, scoop all breast tissue into the cup, then fasten).
  2. If the band feels snug , try a sister size: 36C (band up, cup down).
  3. If the cup feels small , try a cup up in the same band: 34DD.
  4. If the band rides up your back , go one band down and one cup up: 32DD (this is your sister size).

It often takes two or three tries to dial in a new size. Most online bra retailers offer free returns, so this is inexpensive experimentation.

Common Questions

Does the 80% number apply to me? The 80% figure is a population average. If you have unusual breast shape, recent surgery, or are post-mastectomy, the calculator may need to be supplemented with a professional fitting. See our post-mastectomy care guide for specifics.

How often should I re-measure? Every 6–12 months for most adults. After pregnancy, weight change, or hormonal change, re-measure sooner.

Are professional fittings worth it? For a baseline, yes. For ongoing maintenance, no — the calculator and a soft tape give you a more accurate number than most in-store fitters, who are constrained by the inventory on hand.

Summary

The "80%" figure is real, and it isn't a reflection of bodies being "weird." It's a reflection of how rarely we re-measure, how stores vanity-size, and how the sister-size rule is rarely taught. A two-minute measurement and the bra size calculator can put you in the 20% who wear the right size. Then re-measure every 6–12 months and replace bras when the band loses elasticity. Your back, shoulders, and posture will thank you.

References

  1. McGhee, D. E., & Steele, J. R. (2010). Optimising breast support in female patients through correct bra fit. A cross-sectional study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 13 (6), 568–572. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2010.03.003
  2. Greenbaum, A. R., Heslop, T., Morris, J., & Dunn, K. W. (2003). An investigation of the suitability of bra fit in women referred for reduction mammaplasty. British Journal of Plastic Surgery, 56 (3), 230–236. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0007-1226(03)00122-X
  3. Coltman, C. E., Steele, J. R., & McGhee, D. E. (2018). Which bra components contribute to incorrect bra fit in women across a range of breast sizes? Clothing and Textiles Research Journal, 36 (2), 285–298. https://doi.org/10.1177/0887302X17743814
  4. Haworth, L., May, K., Janssen, J., Selfe, J., & Chohan, A. (2022). The impact of breast support garments on fit, support and posture of larger breasted women. Applied Ergonomics, 101 , 103701. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apergo.2022.103701
